title: The month of Assu
hook: in Assu love wells up: how can I meet the Lord (Barah Maha, ang 135)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhadon, and your line: bhadon: doubt. Did you name one doubt, even quietly, to yourself? Bhadon left the bride lost and unsure. Today the rains end, and something in her starts to move. Day five hundred seventy-two.

By Assu, roughly mid-September to mid-October in Punjab, the monsoon has usually blown itself out. The mud dries, the nights cool, and the sky goes a hard, clear blue, the kind where you can suddenly see the far hills that were hidden all summer. Doubt is a lot like the rainy season. While it lasts, you can't see past the next puddle. Then one morning the air clears, and what's left isn't certainty. It's wanting. You can see where you'd like to go, and you have no idea how to get there. That is exactly where Guru Arjan's Assu stanza begins.
screen: `ASSU: THE RAINS END, THE SKY CLEARS.` → `DOUBT GIVES WAY TO WANTING.` → `BUT HOW DO I GET THERE?`

segments.voice: Here's the stanza's opening, in paraphrase: in Assu, love wells up. How can I go and meet the Lord? In Gurmukhi it begins asun prem umaahrraa. Prem is love. Umaahrraa is eagerness, a surge that rises on its own. Then comes the question that gives today its line: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet? Mind and body, the stanza says, are thirsty for a sight of the Beloved. And the bride does something very human. She calls out, O mother, will someone come and bring me to Him? Notice that the Barah Maha doesn't scold her for asking. In the Sikh reading, the question is the first step. Bhadon was confusion, attached to second things. Assu is the same person, now pointed in one direction, even if she doesn't know the road. The stanza then answers, gently. The saints, it says, are the helpers of love, and she falls at their feet. In Sikh life that points to the sangat, the company of people who are also on the way, and to the Guru's word they sing together. Without the Lord, the stanza asks, how can there be peace? There is no other place to go. And it closes on grace: in Assu, those live in peace on whom the Lord shows mercy. So the answer to how isn't a technique. It's company, and longing, and a door opened from the other side. The not-knowing is allowed.
screen: `PREM UMAAHRRAA: LOVE WELLS UP.` · `KIAU MILEE-AI: HOW CAN I MEET?` · `THE SAINTS ARE LOVE'S HELPERS.` · `PEACE COMES BY MERCY.` · then, large: `ASSU: HOW TO MEET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line of longing. Sit comfortably and let your breathing slow. Ask yourself, honestly, what you long for underneath the to-do list. Peace, closeness, forgiveness, a sense of being found. Let it be simple. If you pray, you can carry the stanza's own question on the breath: kiau milee-ai, how can I meet You? If you don't pray, just let the longing be there, without fixing it or explaining it. Breathe in the wanting. Breathe out the hurry. The bell holds the time.
Assu. In Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, Assu is when love wells up and asks how to meet, and the stanza answers: through the holy company, and by mercy.
Your line: assu: how to meet. Today, when you notice yourself wanting something deeper, don't push it away. Ask the question instead, and see who turns up to help. Day five hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: On the Sangrand that begins Assu, gurdwaras that keep the day read Guru Arjan's Assu stanza from the Barah Maha in Raag Majh, often with a short talk on its meaning for the month ahead.

match.prompt: the month of Assu — tap the pairs.

myth: the Assu stanza scolds the bride for not knowing the way
it lets her ask, then answers: the holy company helps, and mercy brings peace.
in the stanza, the bride turns to her mother for help
she calls out, O mother, will someone come and bring me to the Beloved?
the stanza's answer to how is a special technique
its answer is company, longing and grace.

fork.setup: the doubt has cleared and you want to meet the Beloved, but you don't know the way. what does the Assu stanza turn to?
options: wait alone until the longing fades.
the saints, the helpers of love.
a long journey to a faraway shrine.
fork.reveal: the bride falls at the feet of the saints, love's helpers, and the stanza ends: those on whom the Lord shows mercy live in peace.

original.note: Gurmukhi: prem, love. In Assu, the stanza says, prem wells up, umaahrraa, an eager surge.

trapdoor: what you thought: Assu is just the name of a month on the Punjabi calendar.
what it means: in the Barah Maha it's the month when doubt clears into longing, and longing asks how to meet.

what a scholar hears: 'asun prem umaahrraa kiau milee-ai har jaae'; the stanza moves from the bride's question to the saints as love's helpers, and closes 'asoo sukhee vasandeeaa jinaa maiaa har raae'.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, the Assu stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 135)
Barah Maha, Raag Tukhari, Mahalla 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1107)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): varied the hook opener; cut the invented 'water filling a well' gloss of umaahrraa and the unsourced folk-song claim about brides and mothers (the line is the vocative 'maae', O mother); replaced a trapdoor that repeated day 564's word for word; removed a repeated 'first step' line.

Paraphrase of the Assu stanza (asun prem umaahrraa kiau milee-ai har jaae; man tan pi-aas darsan ghanee koee aan milaavai maa-e; sant sahaa-ee prem ke...; asun sukhee vasandee-aa jinaa ma-i-aa har raa-e): please confirm the wording, the Ang (outline says 135; some printings begin the stanza on 134), and the Gurmukhi opening ਅਸੁਨਿ ਪ੍ਰੇਮ ਉਮਾਹੜਾ.
The framing of the bride confiding in her mother as a folk-song convention is offered as context; a Keeper may prefer to leave it out.
Gregorian dates for Assu are approximate (solar month, roughly mid-September to mid-October).
